title: evening-burn-benchlet-log-vikram
content:
Purpose: quick personal tracker for "evening burn" micro-experiments. These are lightweight nightly runs that mimic bursty production traffic (high QPS for 5–15m) to check KV cache behavior, batch sizing, and tail latency under warm/cold cache transitions. Not an official doc — scratchpad for iterations, observations, and small tables I can paste into tickets.

Context and setup:
- Model: gptv-small-quant (50B -> 8-bit tuning) on a single p3.2x-like test instance (approx sim hw).
- Runner: local test harness v0.9.3, with continuous batching enabled and a TTL-based KV cache (ttl=300s unless noted).
- Input mix: 70% short prompts (<=60 tokens), 30% long prompts (~400 tokens) to stress sequence length variable batching.
- Goal metrics: p50/p90/p99 generation latency (ms), token cost estimate, KV hit rate (%), average batch size.

Quick experiment log (evening burn snapshots):
| run | date | duration | batch_max | avg_batch | kv_hit% | p50 | p90 | p99 | notes |
|-----|------|----------|-----------|----------:|--------:|----:|----:|----:|-------|
| EB-01 | 2025-11-04 | 12m | 32 | 8.3 | 12% | 110 | 280 | 1030 | cold start, small cache, default ttl |
| EB-02 | 2025-11-05 | 10m | 64 | 12.1 | 26% | 105 | 240 | 860 | doubled batch_max, slight improvement p99 |
| EB-03 | 2025-11-10 | 15m | 32 | 10.4 | 58% | 95 | 180 | 360 | warmed cache via synthetic prefix reuse; big p99 win |
| EB-04 | 2025-12-01 | 8m | 128 | 18.9 | 33% | 125 | 340 | 1460 | larger batches raised p50, but p99 worse (queueing spike) |
| EB-05 | 2026-01-28 | 14m | 64 | 11.7 | 67% | 92 | 168 | 310 | TTL increase to 600s, repeated queries -> stable low p99 |

Notes / quick observations:
- KV hit rate is the single best predictor of p99 improvements in these bursts; when kv_hit% > 50, p99 drops dramatically.
- Increasing batch_max without controlling burst smoothing increased p50 but introduced queueing outliers that raised p99. Likely because batching delay policy is naive (wait until either batch_max or small-timeout).
- TTL tuning helps for repeated user sessions; for synthetic evening-burn traffic (many near-duplicates), TTL 600s seemed safer. But for memory-constrained nodes, 600s may be too high — need hit/miss cost tradeoff.
- Long prompts blunt batching benefits (memory and compute per request) — mixing small+long pushes system into wider batch variance; average batch size doesn't tell whole story. Consider tracking batch size distribution.

Ideas to try next (short TODOs):
- EB-next-1: instrument batch wait-time distribution and add 95th of wait-time to log (why p99-> high).
- EB-next-2: try hybrid batching policy: max-size 64 + elastic-timeout that shrinks as queue builds.
- EB-next-3: run a controlled warmup (30s synthetic prefix cache fill) vs no-warmup to quantify absolute KV benefit.
- EB-next-4: test TTL 300/450/600/1200 in controlled loop to estimate memory vs latency curve (simple cost model).
- EB-next-5: capture token-cost proxy per run (model tokens * cost-per-token) to show economics of caching.

Rough cost/benefit note for ticket: increasing TTL from 300->600 gave ~30% p99 improvement in evening-burn with only ~12% extra memory usage in profiling run (subjective; need real memory samples). If true, justify a small default TTL bump for burst-heavy customers with an opt-in.

Open questions / flags:
- Are we simulating realistic user stickiness? Evening-burn synthetic duplicates may overestimate KV effect. Need a sampled production trace anonymized.
- How sensitive are these results to model quantization (8-bit vs 4-bit)? Some ops change KV footprint and kernel perf.
- Should we expose batch-wait policy as a tunable default per-customer? Ops complexity vs performance gain tradeoff.

Scratchpad: quick command I used (local harness):
./harness --model gptv-small-quant --burst 1200 --mix short:0.7,long:0.3 --batch-max 64 --ttl 600 --duration 900

Log excerpt (EB-05):
[00:00:12] queued=3 avg_batch=10 wait_p95=12ms kv_hit=0.64 p50=88 p90=162 p99=298
[00:05:21] queued=1 avg_batch=12 wait_p95=9ms kv_hit=0.71 p50=90 p90=160 p99=305

Mindmap of what to capture in formal ticket:
- Short description and rationale (why evening bursts matter)
- Key runs and aggregated metric table (p50/p90/p99, kv_hit, avg_batch)
- Memory delta for TTL changes
- Proposed config changes and rollout plan (A/B, small percentage, monitor p99 and token cost)

Quick sign-off note to self: when prepping for a dedicated-customer demo, run EB sequence with a sampled trace (not synthetic) and collect memory, CPU, and kernel utilization. Paste this summary into PR description.

-- end of scratchpad (Vikram)
